summary: Sets out requirements for protocols that detect lost packets using timers, the only way to be sure a packet is lost when no confirmation arrives. It exists because each protocol implementation tends to reinvent its time-based logic, sometimes badly, and this gives guidance on doing it well. It is a Best Current Practice.

eli5.summary: If a letter has not been confirmed after a while, you assume it got lost. This explains how to pick a sensible waiting time, not too short and not too long.

subtitle: High-level rules for deciding when a packet is lost because no confirmation has arrived in time.

tldr.problem: Protocols can only be sure a packet is lost when time passes without delivery confirmation, yet each protocol has invented its own timer logic with no overarching requirements.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC sets four requirements for a last-resort timeout (the RTO): start no lower than 1 second, base it on multiple recent feedback-time samples, treat a timeout as congestion, and back off exponentially.
tldr.outcome: It applies to unicast communication, gives implementations latitude in the details, and does not update or obsolete any existing RFC.

facts.label: Maximum RTO floor
facts.value: MUST NOT be less than 60 seconds

today: RFC 8961 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 233) published in November 2020. The unit metadata shows no obsoleting or updating RFC, and the text says it does not update or obsolete any existing RFC.

sections.title: Why Time Is the Last Resort
sections.content:
Packet loss is routine in best-effort networks, and protocols detect it for two main reasons: to ensure reliable delivery by retransmitting missing data, and for congestion control, since loss is taken as an implicit sign the sender is going too fast. The RFC leans on the conservative view that loss indicates congestion, which is not always right but has historically served well.

Acknowledgments can tell a sender which data is missing, but they cannot be fully trusted to arrive. The only thing a sender can truly depend on is the passage of time, so a timeout is the ultimate backstop. When the period passes without delivery confirmation, the sender concludes the data was lost.

The length of the wait is a tradeoff between correctness and responsiveness. Waiting too little risks spurious retransmissions and needlessly lowering the sending rate. Waiting too long delays repair and may prolong congestion. TCP, SCTP and SIP each have their own time-based detectors, and the RFC outlines protocol-agnostic requirements as a safe foundation.
sections.eli5: When no answer comes back, the only thing you can really count on is the clock. If the clock runs out, you assume the message was lost.

sections.title: Context and Scope
sections.content:
The RFC admits it is unusual: normally requirements come first and protocols follow, but the IETF derived many loss detectors before it knew how to write such requirements. Now it can separate what matters for network safety from small details. It should be read as the default case, not one-size-fits-all guidance. It does not update or obsolete any existing RFC, and future time-based loss detection mechanisms SHOULD follow it. Inconsistencies MUST be explained and gather consensus.

The scope statements are:

  • Only loss detection, not other uses of timers such as pacing.
  • Only the primary or last-resort detector, even when other mechanisms such as selective acknowledgments also exist.
  • Only endpoint-to-endpoint unicast. A host talking to several addresses needs an independent detector for each one. Reliable multicast is out.
  • Sharing loss detection state across flows is outside the scope.
sections.eli5: These are rules for the main safety-net timer between two computers, not for every clock a program might use.

sections.title: The Initial Timeout
sections.content:
The RFC calls the time between sending a packet and deciding it is lost the retransmission timeout or RTO, even if the packet will not be retransmitted.

Requirement 1: with no knowledge of path latency, the initial RTO MUST be conservatively set to no less than 1 second. Correctness matters most when the network is unknown. Premature loss detection can trigger spurious retransmits into a possibly congested network, can needlessly cut the sending rate when it is already low, and can muddy the first latency sample that serves as a baseline. The 1 second figure comes from the analysis of round-trip times in Appendix A of RFC 6298.
sections.eli5: Before you know how long the trip takes, wait at least a full second. Giving up too early would make things worse.

sections.title: Setting the Timeout from Feedback Time
sections.content:
The RFC frames the expected delay as feedback time (FT) rather than just round-trip time, since a reply can include extra processing time. For example, a DNS resolver answering from its cache replies faster than one that must ask authoritative servers. Requirement 2 has four parts:

  • (a) The RTO SHOULD be based on multiple observations of FT. TCP's exponentially weighted moving average satisfies this. The RFC does not fix the number of samples or how they age out. New protocols are encouraged to make feedback hard for attackers to spoof.
  • (b) FT SHOULD be sampled at least once per RTT, or as often as data is exchanged if that is less frequent.
  • (c) FT MAY be taken from non-data exchanges such as keepalives.
  • (d) The mechanism MUST NOT use ambiguous samples. If two copies of a packet were sent and one confirmation arrives, it is unclear which copy it answers, so neither sample is used and the RTO is not updated. If the sender can tell them apart, as with the TCP timestamp option, the sample may be used.
sections.eli5: Keep timing how long answers really take, and use many recent times, not one. If you cannot tell which of two identical letters got the reply, do not use that time at all.

sections.title: Reacting to a Timeout
sections.content:
Requirement 3: loss found by the RTO MUST be taken as a sign of congestion and the sending rate adapted by a standard mechanism. For example, TCP collapses its congestion window to one packet. An exception applies if an IETF-standardized mechanism determines that the loss was not congestion, such as corruption, and the action may be reversed if such a mechanism later shows the cause was not congestion.

Requirement 4: each time the RTO detects a loss, its value MUST be exponentially backed off so the next firing needs a longer interval. The backoff SHOULD be removed after a successful transmission of non-retransmitted data, or after an RTO passes without detecting more losses. A maximum RTO MAY be set, but it MUST NOT be less than 60 seconds. The same non-congestion exception applies, and both requirements are there for network safety.
sections.eli5: If the timer runs out, slow down, because the road may be jammed. Each time it runs out again, wait longer before the next try.

sections.title: Discussion and Security
sections.content:
Research cited by the RFC suggests the tension between responsiveness and correctness is fundamental. A more aggressive RTO finds real loss sooner but wrongly declares more packets lost, and each declared loss triggers a congestion response. Mechanisms such as Eifel, F-RTO and DSACK can detect mistaken loss decisions and let a sender lean toward responsiveness.

The RFC notes that some TCP implementations use non-standard RTO details, such as a steady-state minimum below 1 second, and it knows of no large-scale network safety problems from that. This is why no minimum RTO is specified. Because the requirements still insist on exponential backoff and a rate reduction, they fail safely.

On security, the document does not alter the security properties of time-based loss detection and points to RFC 6298 for the TCP context. It has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: Being jumpy finds real losses faster but also raises false alarms. The rules make false alarms cost something, so nobody gets too jumpy.

items.title: 1. Start cautious
items.text: Initial RTO MUST be no less than 1 second.

items.title: 2. Learn from samples
items.text: Use multiple feedback-time observations, never ambiguous ones.

items.title: 3. Treat loss as congestion
items.text: Adapt the sending rate with a standard mechanism.

items.title: 4. Back off
items.text: Exponentially lengthen the RTO after each loss; any maximum MUST NOT be below 60 seconds.
